## Why This Is Asked
This question tests practical debugging skills, Helm templating understanding, and production deployment best practices. Engineering teams need team members who can troubleshoot real deployment issues effectively.

## Expected Answer
The candidate should explain: 1) Verify image exists in the configured registry, 2) Check imagePullSecrets configuration, 3) Use semantic versioning instead of 'latest' tag, 4) Set appropriate pull policies for production stability, 5) Use Helm template rendering commands to debug configuration issues.

## Code Example
```yaml
# values.yaml
image:
  repository: my-registry.com/my-service
  tag: v1.2.3
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent
  pullSecrets: [regcred]

# deployment.yaml
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      imagePullSecrets:
        - name: regcred
      containers:
        - name: my-service
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
          imagePullPolicy: {{ .Values.image.pullPolicy }}
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical mastery of Kubernetes resource management, debugging OOM scenarios, and using native primitives to prevent recurrence.

## Key Concepts
- Resource requests and limits configuration
- OOMKilled signals and container memory pressure diagnostics
- Namespace LimitRange and default resource enforcement
- Safe deployment strategies with minimal service disruption

## Code Example
```yaml
# Deployment patch to add memory resources
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: prod
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: your-image
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "256Mi"
          limits:
            memory: "512Mi"
```

```yaml
# Namespace LimitRange for default constraints
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-mem-limits
  namespace: prod
spec:
  limits:
  - default:
      memory: "512Mi"
    defaultRequest:
      memory: "256Mi"
    type: Container
```

This question probes ability to design policy-driven multi-tenant governance on Kubernetes, with clear separation, inheritance semantics, and observable enforcement.

## Key Concepts
- CRD-driven policy modeling, inheritance, and conflict resolution
- RBAC/PSP (or PodSecurityPolicy migration) and StorageClass constraints translation
- Auditing, metrics, and observable policy evaluation

## Code Example
```yaml
# sketch of TenantGovernance CRD spec
apiVersion: governance.example/v1
kind: TenantGovernance
metadata:
  name: prod-tenant
spec:
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      tenant: prod
  imagePolicy:
    allowedRegistries: ["registry.company.com"]
  storagePolicy:
    requireEncryption: true
    allowedStorageClasses: ["gp2-encrypted"]
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle conflicting policies across overlapping namespaces?
- What metrics would you expose for policy efficacy and drift?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical use of native autoscaling with realistic cluster constraints and verification paths.

## Key Concepts
- HorizontalPodAutoscaler
- Metrics Server
- CPU requests/limits and resource budgeting
- kubectl-based verification

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v1
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: inventory-hpa
  namespace: warehouse
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: inventory
  minReplicas: 1
  maxReplicas: 10
  targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 60
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you monitor and interpret HPA behavior under peak load? Which metrics and commands would you watch?
- If memory becomes the bottleneck instead of CPU, how would you adapt the approach?

questions.explanation:
## Diagnosis Approach

- Check pod logs and events for network-related errors
- Test connectivity using `kubectl exec` with `ping`, `curl`, `nslookup`
- Examine CNI plugin logs (Calico, Flannel, Cilium)
- Verify network policies aren't blocking required traffic

## Cluster-Level Investigation

- Check kube-proxy mode and iptables rules
- Monitor node network interfaces and bandwidth
- Verify CoreDNS functionality and pod DNS resolution
- Check for IP address exhaustion in the cluster

## Resolution Strategies

- Adjust network policies to allow required traffic
- Scale CoreDNS deployment if experiencing DNS timeouts
- Configure proper resource limits for network-intensive pods
- Implement network monitoring with Prometheus/Grafana

## Tools and Commands

```bash
# Check pod network connectivity
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- ping <service>

# Examine network policies
kubectl get networkpolicies -A

# Check CNI status
caliclctl node status
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Demonstrates runtime config rotation using Kubernetes primitives, ensuring zero downtime by triggering controlled rollouts when ConfigMaps change.

## Key Concepts
- Immutable ConfigMaps
- Mounting ConfigMap as files in a Pod
- Triggering rollouts via PodTemplate annotations
- CI validation: rollout status and smoke checks

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: web-app-config
  namespace: web
immutable: true
data:
  flags.yaml: |
    featureX: true
    featureY: false
```
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
  namespace: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
      annotations:
        configHash: ""
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web-app
        image: your-image:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config
          mountPath: /config
          readOnly: true
      volumes:
      - name: config
        configMap:
          name: web-app-config
          items:
          - key: flags.yaml
            path: flags.yaml
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you automate the hash calculation and Deployment patch in CI?
- What tests would you add to CI to ensure no downtime during rotation?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This tests a beginner-friendly blue-green pattern, emphasizing safe traffic switch, rollback, and observability using native primitives (Deployments, Services, Ingress) without external controllers.

## Key Concepts
- Blue-Green deployments
- Deployments and Services selectors
- Ingress-based traffic routing
- Readiness probes and smoke tests

## Code Example
```yaml
# web-app-v1 Deployment (snippet)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app-v1
  labels: {app: web-app, version: v1}
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: web-app, version: v1}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web-app
        image: myrepo/web-app:v1
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8080}
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8080}
```
```yaml
# web-svc-v2 Service (snippet)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-svc-v2
spec:
  selector: {app: web-app, version: v2}
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080
    protocol: TCP
    name: http
```
```yaml
# Ingress (snippet) routing to green service
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web-ingress
spec:
  rules:
  - http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web-svc-v2
            port:
              number: 80
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you automate health checks and rollback on CI failure?
- How would you handle database migrations during blue-green switch?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to design practical credential rotation automation in a multi-tenant cluster, including external secret stores, per-namespace scoping, and safe rollout semantics.

## Key Concepts

- CRD/controller patterns
- Secret management and versioning
- Safe rolling updates and observability

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: secretrotationpolicies.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            properties:
              rotationInterval:
                type: string
              mappings:
                type: array
                items:
                  type: object
                  properties:
                    secretName:
                      type: string
                    vaultPath:
                      type: string
                    targetKey:
                      type: string
              rollout:
                type: object
                properties:
                  type:
                    type: string
                  maxUnavailable:
                    type: integer
  scope: Namespaced
  names:
    plural: secretrotationpolicies
    singular: secretrotationpolicy
    kind: SecretRotationPolicy
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you test vault rotation and ensure no service disruption?
- How would you handle partial failures when tokens cannot be fetched?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical Kuberenetes scoping basics: namespace quotas, limit ranges, and CI validation without external tools.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped resource management
- LimitRange vs ResourceQuota)
- Validation via kubectl apply --dry-run
- CI integration for quota enforcement

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: web-limits
  namespace: web
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    max:
      cpu: "1"
      memory: "512Mi"
    min:
      cpu: "100m"
      memory: "64Mi"
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: "200m"
      memory: "256Mi"
```

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: web-quota
  namespace: web
spec:
hard:
  pods: "5"
  requests.cpu: "5"
  requests.memory: "4Gi"
  limits.cpu: "5"
  limits.memory: "8Gi"
```

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
  namespace: web
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web-app
        image: nginx:alpine
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "2"
            memory: "1Gi"
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you verify quota enforcement in CI across environments?
- How would you adjust defaults for bursty workloads while keeping overall limits safe?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests real-world ephemeral env handling with safety and observability.

## Key Concepts
- Namespaced lifecycle, Finalizers
- EnvLifecyclePolicy CRD
- ResourceQuota/LimitRange per-NS
- TTL-based cleanup and PR-driven teardown
- Observability via metrics and events

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: standard.example/v1
kind: EnvLifecyclePolicy
metadata:
  name: ephemeral-pr
spec:
  ttl: 48h
  quotas:
    hard:
      requests.cpu: 2
      requests.memory: 4Gi
  cleanupPolicy: DeleteNamespace
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle failure in deploying the test stack during namespace creation?
- How would you audit and chargeback per-namespace usage?
